docs.text: AutoEdits Editor The Auto Edits Editor allows you to specify automatic edits that can be applied to applicable data on one or more meters. This is especially useful if you have data imported or entered every month for which you know you have to change specific detail(s), characteristic(s), or analysis.

docs.title: Key Characteristics
docs.text:
• Auto edits apply to all applicable data, regardless of the status of the record; that is, if the data is closed, an auto edit still applies if the data meets the condition of the auto edit and a PPA is also created.
  • Auto edits do not apply to meter data that is created or edited from the Auto Estimate service or Master Allocations.
  • To set up an auto edit: Go to Setup Meter Auto Edits Editor .
  • When Auto Edit criteria are defined on more than one tab, the Auto Edits are applied in the following order: Auto edits defined on tabs that do not trigger a recalculation Auto edits defined on tabs that trigger a recalculation of the correlation factors applicable to that meter; correlation factors are then recalculated Auto edits defined on tabs that trigger a recalculation of volume and mass; volume and mass are then recalculated Gas Auto Edits Upon import of meter data, FLOWCAL attempts to apply the Auto Edit to each periodic record that is imported.
  • On edits, FLOWCAL attempts to apply the Auto Edit to each periodic record that is within the Contract Month of the data that is modified.
  • For meter characteristic Auto Edits, the Auto Edit only applies to characteristic records within the Contract Month.

docs.text: Densitometer Editor The Densitometer Editor allows users to create densitometers that can be assigned to meters. Densitometers can be set up to either apply a particular density meter factor (DMF) to a meter or validate the meter’s DMF at import time.

docs.title: Key Characteristics

docs.title: Gas Distribution and End Users
docs.text: Describes the final stage of natural gas flow from pipeline to end users. Explains distribution systems, various customer categories including residential, commercial, and industrial, and how measurement occurs at delivery points.

docs.title: Distribution Systems and Companies
docs.text:
Natural gas distribution systems transport gas from transmission pipelines to end users. Distribution companies operate these local systems and are responsible for delivering gas to customers. Examples include CenterPoint Energy, Atmos Energy, and others. Distribution companies own and operate the infrastructure from the city gate (where gas enters from transmission pipelines) through local distribution networks to individual customer connections.

  • Distribution companies operate local gas delivery networks.
  • Gas flows from transmission pipelines to distribution systems.
  • Distribution infrastructure extends from city gates to customers.
  • Major distributors include CenterPoint Energy, Atmos Energy, and others.
  • Distribution companies manage local pipeline infrastructure.

docs.title: Measurement at Distribution Points
docs.text:
Measurement occurs at various points in the distribution system where gas is delivered to or transferred between customers. City gates represent delivery points where transmission company gas enters distribution company systems. At these gates and throughout the distribution system, meters measure the volume of gas being delivered, ensuring accurate billing and ownership accounting. Measurement points occur whenever there is a change in ownership or at regulatory checkpoints.

  • City gate meters measure gas entering distribution systems.
  • Measurement ensures accurate billing to end users.
  • Meters track ownership transfers between companies.
  • Distribution point meters measure gas delivered to customers.
  • Regulatory requirements mandate measurement at key points.

docs.title: End User Categories and Usage
docs.text:
Natural gas is delivered to diverse end-user categories. Residential customers include individual homes where gas is used for heating and appliances. Commercial customers include businesses that use gas for operations. Industrial customers include large-scale operations such as agricultural drying operations that require significant gas volumes. Some very large industrial users may receive gas directly from transmission pipelines rather than through distribution networks. City gate deliveries serve municipal distribution systems that deliver gas to residential and commercial end users.

  • Residential users: individual homes for heating and appliances.
  • Commercial users: businesses for heating and operations.
  • Industrial users: large operations requiring high gas volumes.
  • Agricultural operations: use gas for crop drying.
  • City gates: deliver gas to municipal distribution systems.
  • End-user categories determine distribution requirements.

docs.title: Gathering Systems
docs.text: Explains how gathering systems collect and consolidate natural gas from multiple production wells into larger pipelines for transport. Describes the role of gathering companies, quality management, and the transition from well-site production to major pipeline infrastructure.

docs.title: Purpose of Gathering Systems
docs.text:
A gathering system collects natural gas from multiple production wells and consolidates it into a larger pipe for transportation. Natural gas cannot be trucked as a liquid and must be transported via pipeline. Gathering systems bridge the gap between individual well sites and major transmission pipelines. Multiple wells feed into progressively larger pipes that combine and direct the gas stream toward processing facilities and major pipeline systems.

  • Gathering systems collect gas from multiple production wells.
  • Gas consolidates from smaller to larger pipes for transport.
  • Natural gas requires pipeline transport (cannot be trucked).
  • Gathering systems connect well sites to major pipelines.
  • A gathering system serves as a collection and consolidation network.

docs.title: Gathering Companies and Ownership
docs.text:
Gathering systems are operated by specialized gathering companies that are separate from the production companies. These companies may take ownership of the gas after it exits the well meters, or they may be contracted to simply transport and manage the flow. Gathering companies are paid for their services and manage the quality and movement of gas through their system. At the point where gas enters a gathering system, ownership may transfer from the production company to the gathering company, creating a measurement and accounting point.

  • Gathering systems are operated by specialized gathering companies.
  • Gathering companies may own the gas or work on a service basis.
  • Ownership transfers may occur at the gathering system entry point.
  • Gathering companies manage quality and gas movement.
  • Measurement points track ownership transfers for accounting.

docs.title: Gathering and Pipeline Quality Requirements
docs.text:
As gas moves through gathering systems toward major pipelines, it must meet quality specifications. Pipelines have strict requirements for gas quality including BTU content, water content, and hydrogen sulfide levels. If gas does not meet pipeline A's specifications, it may need to be routed to pipeline B, treated to improve quality, or processed further. Gathering systems manage this quality control and routing based on pipeline requirements and current specifications.

  • Pipelines have quality requirements: BTU content, water, hydrogen sulfide levels.
  • Gathering systems ensure gas meets pipeline specifications.
  • Non-conforming gas may be routed to alternative pipelines.
  • Gas may require additional treatment before pipeline acceptance.
  • Quality management is integral to gathering system operations.

docs.title: Meter Calibration and Testing
docs.text: Explains the critical importance of meter calibration, inspection, and testing in the measurement process. Describes how TestIt system tracks meter maintenance schedules, test results, and quality assurance to ensure data accuracy in flow measurements.

docs.title: Meter Calibration and Inspection Requirements
docs.text:
All meters used in hydrocarbon measurement must be calibrated and regularly inspected. Operators must conduct inspections of meter components to ensure proper function. For orifice meters (common in gas measurement), the orifice plate must be visually inspected to verify it remains in good condition and may need to be replaced if it shows wear or damage. These inspections are not random but are contractually required on defined schedules, ensuring systematic maintenance of measurement accuracy.

  • Meter calibration is required for all measurement points.
  • Regular inspections verify proper meter function.
  • Orifice plates in orifice meters must be inspected.
  • Orifice plates may need replacement due to wear.
  • Inspections follow contractually-defined schedules.

docs.title: The TestIt System for Quality Assurance
docs.text:
TestIt is a comprehensive system used to track and manage the maintenance and testing of meters. It maintains schedules for all meter tests, ensuring inspections occur on defined intervals rather than randomly. TestIt records meter test results, maintains inspection records, tracks samples collected for gas quality analysis, and documents the status of meter maintenance. This systematic approach to meter management is critical to ensuring data quality, as poor meter maintenance leads to unreliable measurements that propagate through calculations and reports.

  • TestIt tracks meter maintenance schedules and test results.
  • Meter testing follows contractual schedules.
  • Test results are recorded and maintained for audit.
  • Gas samples are collected for quality analysis.
  • TestIt ensures systematic, not random, meter maintenance.
  • Quality meter data is foundational to accurate calculations.

docs.title: Data Quality and Measurement Integrity
docs.text:

Poor data from improperly maintained meters produces unreliable results. As the saying goes in data management, 'garbage in, garbage out.' FLOWCAL relies on receiving quality meter data; if the source meters are not properly maintained and calibrated, all calculations and reports will be compromised. Therefore, TestIt's role in ensuring meter quality is vital to the entire flow measurement process.

  • Data quality depends on meter calibration and maintenance.
  • Poor meter maintenance leads to unreliable measurements.
  • Measurement errors propagate through all calculations.
  • FLOWCAL depends on quality input data.
  • TestIt ensures measurement integrity throughout the system.

docs.title: What Is a Meter
docs.text:
In FLOWCAL, everything originates from meter data. A meter is a physical device installed where product is pulled from the ground or transferred through a pipeline, and it measures volume - how much product is moving. A FLOCON filter is attached to the meter and captures the raw data based on the meter's pressure base at the time of measurement.

  • A meter is a physical device that measures product volume as it is pulled from the ground or transferred through a pipeline.
  • A FLOCON filter attaches to the meter and captures raw measurement data.

docs.title: Meter Types and Characteristics
docs.text:
Different meter types - such as Coriolis or turbine - calculate flow differently, so each meter's characteristics must be defined. Two key characteristics are the pressure base and the temperature base: the temperature of the product, the meter's own temperature, and the pressure base together determine how raw data is converted into flow.

  • Meter types include Coriolis and turbine, each with its own calculation method.
  • Pressure base and temperature base are core characteristics assigned to a meter.
  • Both product temperature and meter temperature feed into the flow calculation.

docs.title: Pipeline Infrastructure and Compression
docs.text: Describes natural gas pipeline infrastructure including quality requirements, compressor stations, line pack storage in pipelines, and how compression maintains gas flow across long distances. Explains the fuel consumption measurement needs for accurate gain/loss accounting.

docs.title: Pipeline Quality Requirements
docs.text:
Natural gas pipelines have strict quality requirements that the gas must meet before acceptance. These requirements include specifications for BTU content (energy density), water content, and hydrogen sulfide levels. Gas that does not meet these specifications cannot enter a particular pipeline and must either be treated to improve quality or routed to a different pipeline with less stringent requirements. Pipeline operators enforce these standards to ensure product quality and system integrity throughout the distribution network.

  • Pipelines have strict quality specifications for accepted gas.
  • Key quality parameters: BTU content, water content, hydrogen sulfide.
  • Non-conforming gas cannot enter pipelines.
  • Gas may be treated to meet quality requirements.
  • Quality management protects product integrity and system reliability.

docs.title: Compressor Stations and Pressure Management
docs.text:
As natural gas moves through pipelines over long distances, pressure decreases due to friction and loss of potential energy. Compressor stations are installed along pipelines to maintain adequate pressure and keep the gas moving forward. Compressor stations also enable line pack operations where gas is deliberately pressurized into the pipeline for temporary storage. There are pressure limits on pipes, and compressor stations manage pressurization to keep gas flowing while respecting these mechanical limits.

  • Compressor stations maintain pressure along pipelines.
  • Pressure decreases naturally as gas travels distance.
  • Compressors increase pressure to maintain flow velocity.
  • Compressors enable line pack storage within pipelines.
  • Pressure limits on pipelines constrain compressor operations.

docs.title: Line Pack and Strategic Gas Storage
docs.text:
Natural gas is highly compressible, allowing large volumes to be temporarily stored within pipelines themselves through line pack operations. Additional gas is intentionally pumped into pipelines in anticipation of high demand periods, such as before cold weather events when heating demand increases. FLOWCAL uses line pack meters to track the volume of gas stored in pipelines, which can represent significant financial value. Line pack is managed through strategic use of compressor stations to pack gas in advance of predictable demand surges.

  • Natural gas's compressibility enables pipeline storage (line pack).
  • Gas is packed in advance of high demand periods.
  • Cold weather events drive line pack strategy for heating demand.
  • Line pack meters track stored gas volume and value.
  • Strategic packing maintains supply reliability during demand peaks.

docs.title: Compressor Fuel Consumption and Measurement
docs.text:
Compressor stations use fuel (typically natural gas) to operate. Ideally, fuel consumption is measured directly with fuel meters. However, in some cases, fuel measurement is expensive and the volume consumed is small, so measurement is not implemented. Instead, fuel consumption should be calculated using FLOWCAL's calculated meter functionality based on compressor specifications and operating parameters. Accurate measurement or calculation of compressor fuel consumption is essential for gain/loss accounting, as fuel burned represents gas leaving the system that must be accounted for to explain total flow changes.

  • Compressor stations consume fuel for operation.
  • Fuel measurement is ideal but sometimes economically impractical.
  • Calculated meters can estimate fuel consumption.
  • Fuel consumption must be accounted for in gain/loss calculations.
  • Without fuel accounting, unexplained losses will appear in the system.

docs.title: Separation Processes and Well Stream Factors
docs.text: Describes the separation process used to isolate natural gas from water, sediment, and natural gas liquids in raw extracted streams. Explains well stream factors and how they account for measurement impurities to ensure accurate gas volume calculations.

docs.title: Separation at the Well Site
docs.text:
Raw hydrocarbon streams extracted from production wells contain a mixture of natural gas, water, sediment, rocks, dirt, and natural gas liquids. At the well site or shortly after, a separator is used to begin the separation process. The separator uses gravity and physical properties to separate the components: water and sediment settle to the bottom, while natural gas rises to the top. However, not all well sites have separators, particularly at the initial production point.

  • Separators are used to separate mixed hydrocarbon streams into components.
  • Water and sediment separate by gravity to the bottom of the separator.
  • Natural gas, being lighter, rises to the top.
  • Not all well sites have separators installed.
  • Separators may be permanently installed or mobile (test separators).

docs.title: Well Stream Factors and Measurement Accuracy
docs.text:
When meters are installed in unseparated or partially separated streams, they measure everything present (gas, liquids, solids) rather than just pure natural gas. This causes over-measurement. Well stream factors account for this inaccuracy by calculating what portion of the measured volume is actually pure natural gas versus impurities. For example, a meter might measure 1000 cubic feet of fluid, but after accounting for the well stream factor, only 980 cubic feet is determined to be pure natural gas. This factor is calculated using test separators and provided to FLOWCAL for accurate flow calculations.

  • Well stream factors correct for over-measurement in unseparated streams.
  • Test separators are used to calculate well stream factors.
  • Factors account for the presence of water, liquids, and solids.
  • A measured volume of 1000 cubic feet might actually represent 980 cubic feet of pure gas.
  • FLOWCAL uses well stream factors in flow calculations and royalty determinations.

docs.title: Multi-Stage Separation
docs.text:
Separation continues at multiple points in the hydrocarbon production process. Before gas enters major pipelines, comprehensive separation is performed to remove water, solids, and natural gas liquids. Natural gas liquids (NGLs) are valuable products that must be separated because they are worth more than methane alone. Multiple separators at different stages ensure progressive purification of the gas stream before pipeline entry.

  • Separation occurs at multiple points in the production process.
  • Progressive separation increases gas purity at each stage.
  • Water, solids, and natural gas liquids are removed before pipeline entry.
  • Natural gas liquids have higher value and are separated for independent sale.
  • Quality specifications must be met before pipeline acceptance.

docs.title: FLOWCAL Data Journey Overview
docs.text: A high-level walkthrough of how a new user moves through FLOWCAL end to end: security setup (users and groups), creating a liquid product/meter, building out locations and tickets, validating incoming meter data, resolving exceptions, closing meters, routing changes through PPA approval, manually importing data, and rolling up results into reports.

docs.title: Security: Users and Groups
docs.text:
Access to FLOWCAL is controlled through users and groups. Administrators create groups, each with a different privilege level, and then assign individual users to the group that matches the access they need.

  • Users are created individually and then assigned to one or more groups.
  • Groups are created with distinct privilege levels to control what a user can access or do in FLOWCAL.

docs.title: End-to-End Data Flow
docs.text:
After security is configured, the basic FLOWCAL workflow is: create a liquid product and meter (with a base pressure and base temperature), create the meter's location and tickets, assign characteristics to the meter, receive meter data, and validate whether the incoming data is good. Data that fails validation closes on an exception, which must be resolved. Once data looks good, the meter is closed for the period; any later change to a closed meter (such as an equation change) requires approval through the PPA (post-processing approval) workflow. Data can also be brought in through manual imports, after which results are rolled up and viewed in reports.

  • Liquid product/meter setup requires a base pressure and base temperature.
  • Core setup order: meter -> location -> tickets -> characteristics -> meter data -> validation.
  • Data that fails validation closes on an exception and must be resolved before the meter can be closed.
  • Changes to an already-closed meter (e.g. an equation change) require PPA approval.
  • Manual imports bring data into FLOWCAL outside of automated collection.
  • Rolled-up data is the basis for FLOWCAL reports.

docs.title: Hydrocarbon Fundamentals
docs.text: Introduction to hydrocarbons and the three primary fluid types measured in the energy industry: crude oil, natural gas, and water. Explains how these fluids are extracted from underground formations in mixed states and separated at various stages.

docs.title: What Are Hydrocarbons
docs.text:
Hydrocarbons are compounds made up of hydrogen and carbon elements. In the energy industry, three primary types of fluids are extracted and measured: crude oil (heavier hydrocarbon products), natural gas (lighter hydrocarbon mixture), and water (co-produced with hydrocarbons). These fluids are initially extracted as a mixture from underground formations and must be separated at various stages to be processed and transported.

  • Hydrocarbons are hydrogen and carbon compounds extracted from underground formations.
  • Three primary fluids in energy industry: crude oil, natural gas, and water.
  • These fluids are initially extracted in mixed form.
  • Separation processes are used at various stages to separate different hydrocarbon types.

docs.title: Natural Gas as a Hydrocarbon Mixture
docs.text:
Natural gas is not a pure single compound but rather a mixture of different hydrocarbon compounds. Methane is the largest component of natural gas, but it can also include ethane, propane, butane, and other compounds. The exact composition varies depending on the geological formation from which it is extracted.

  • Natural gas is a mixture of hydrocarbon compounds, not a single pure substance.
  • Methane is the largest component of natural gas.
  • Natural gas can contain ethane, propane, butane, and other compounds.
  • Composition varies by geological source.

docs.title: Mixed Extraction from Underground
docs.text:
When hydrocarbons are initially extracted from underground formations, they come up mixed with other substances including water, sediment, rocks, dirt, hydrogen sulfide, and natural gas liquids. This mixed stream must be separated to isolate and quantify each product type for measurement, quality control, and regulatory purposes.

  • Extracted hydrocarbon streams are initially mixed with water, sediment, and other materials.
  • Hydrogen sulfide and other compounds may be present in raw extractions.
  • Natural gas liquids are valuable co-products that must be separated.
  • Separation and purification are necessary for accurate measurement and quality control.

docs.title: Natural Gas Measurement Process Overview
docs.text: Comprehensive overview of natural gas measurement through the entire production and distribution chain from extraction to end user. Shows how measurement occurs at critical points including production wells, separators, gathering systems, pipelines, and distribution systems, and where FLOWCAL fits in managing this measurement data.

docs.title: The Complete Natural Gas Flow Process
docs.text:
The natural gas measurement process spans the entire value chain from underground extraction to delivery to end users. It begins at production wells where natural gas is extracted from underground formations. Gas then moves through separation processes to remove water and other compounds, into gathering systems that consolidate multiple wells, through transmission pipelines to distribution systems, and finally to end users. Measurement occurs at multiple points throughout this chain wherever there is a change in ownership or regulatory requirement. FLOWCAL's role is to receive data from these measurement points, perform calculations, and provide reports.

  • Measurement spans production, processing, transmission, and distribution.
  • Natural gas flows from wells to consumers through multiple stages.
  • Measurement occurs at ownership transfer and regulatory points.
  • FLOWCAL integrates measurement data from multiple systems.
  • FLOWCAL calculations provide accurate volume and royalty reporting.

docs.title: Measurement Points in the Process
docs.text:
Critical measurement points in natural gas flow include: the well head (though often with inaccurate data requiring well stream factors); after separation processing; at gathering system entry points; at major pipeline intersections and custody transfer points; at compressor stations (for fuel consumption); at pipeline inlet and outlets; at distribution city gates; and at end-user delivery points. Each measurement point serves specific accounting or regulatory purposes. Where ownership changes, measurement ensures accurate billing and royalty payments. Where regulatory requirements exist, measurement provides compliance documentation.

  • Well head: initial measurement (often with well stream factors).
  • After separation: cleaner gas streams for more accurate measurement.
  • Gathering system: consolidation points for multiple wells.
  • Custody transfer points: ownership change accounting.
  • Compressor stations: fuel consumption tracking.
  • Distribution city gates: wholesale-to-retail transition.
  • End-user meters: billing and delivery verification.

docs.title: FLOWCAL's Role in the Measurement Process
docs.text:
FLOWCAL is not a measurement device but rather a data management and calculation system. It receives measurement data from meters installed at various points in the natural gas system. Using this data, FLOWCAL performs calculations to determine actual volume flow, applies corrections like well stream factors, tracks line pack volumes, calculates compressor fuel consumption, and produces reports for billing, royalty accounting, and regulatory compliance. FLOWCAL integrates with TestIt and other Quorum solutions to provide a complete measurement and data management ecosystem.

  • FLOWCAL receives data from multiple meter sources.
  • FLOWCAL performs calculations on raw measurement data.
  • FLOWCAL applies well stream factors for measurement accuracy.
  • FLOWCAL manages line pack volume tracking.
  • FLOWCAL supports calculated meters for cost-effective measurement.
  • FLOWCAL produces reports for accounting and compliance.
  • FLOWCAL integrates with TestIt for data quality assurance.

docs.title: Well Extraction and Hydraulic Fracturing
docs.text: Explains the two primary methods for extracting natural gas from underground: conventional drilling and hydraulic fracturing. Details how hydraulic fracturing uses water and sand at high pressure to fracture tight rock formations and release trapped gas.

docs.title: Production Wells and Extraction Methods
docs.text:
A production well is an area where natural gas is extracted from the ground. There are two primary extraction methods: conventional wells where operators drill straight down through the formation, and fracking (hydraulic fracturing) operations used when conventional methods are insufficient. The extraction method depends on the geological characteristics of the formation and how the gas is held in the rock.

  • Production wells are the starting point for hydrocarbon extraction.
  • Conventional drilling: drilling straight down through the formation.
  • Hydraulic fracturing (fracking): used for tight or resistant formations.
  • Choice of method depends on geological formation characteristics.

docs.title: Hydraulic Fracturing (Fracking) Process
docs.text:
Hydraulic fracturing is a technique used to extract gas from tight rock formations where conventional drilling is ineffective. The process involves pumping water and sand (called proppant) along with chemicals down into the well at very high pressure. The water fractures the rock by force, and the sand props open the fractures in the rock. This creates pathways for the gas to move out of the rock into the wellbore pipe, where it can be produced. The term 'hydraulic fracturing' comes from the use of water (hydraulic) to fracture the rock.

  • Hydraulic fracturing extracts gas from tight rock formations.
  • Process pumps water, sand (proppant), and chemicals down the well.
  • Water is pumped at very high pressure to fracture the rock.
  • Sand props open the fractures, creating gas flow pathways.
  • Gas moves from rock formation into the wellbore for production.
  • Alternative to conventional drilling for resistant formations.

docs.title: Drilling Completion and Production
docs.text:
Whether using conventional or hydraulic fracturing methods, a pipe is installed in the well to capture the extracted gas. In some conventional approaches, explosives may be used to shoot holes in both the pipe and rock to allow gas flow. Once fractures or holes are established, gas flows through these pathways into the pipe and is produced at the surface for processing.

  • Pipe is installed in the wellbore to capture extracted gas.
  • Conventional methods may use explosives to create flow paths.
  • Fractures provide pathways for gas to reach the wellbore.
  • Gas flows through established pathways into the collection pipe.
